module_title: Chemical Bonding Basics: Octet Rule & VSEPR Theory (Detailed Foundational)
introduction: This foundational level establishes why atoms combine to form molecules. It covers the classical Kossel-Lewis approach (Octet Rule), the classification of bonds (Ionic, Covalent, Coordinate), and the vital VSEPR theory which dictates the 3D shapes of molecules based on electron repulsion.

core_concepts.title: The Octet Rule (Kossel-Lewis Approach)
core_concepts.description:
Atoms interact to form chemical bonds either by losing, gaining, or sharing electrons to attain the stable, fully filled valence shell configuration of the nearest noble gas (usually 8 electrons, an octet). 
Exceptions to the Octet Rule:
1. Incomplete Octet: Central atom has fewer than 8 electrons (e.g., $BeCl_2$ has 4e-, $BF_3$ has 6e-). Acts as Lewis Acids.
2. Expanded Octet: Central atom has more than 8 electrons due to available empty d-orbitals (e.g., $PCl_5$ has 10e-, $SF_6$ has 12e-).
3. Odd-Electron Molecules: Molecules with an odd total number of electrons (e.g., $NO$, $NO_2$, $ClO_2$). These are highly reactive and paramagnetic.

core_concepts.title: Types of Chemical Bonds
core_concepts.description:
1. Ionic (Electrovalent) Bond: Complete transfer of electrons from a metal (low Ionization Energy) to a non-metal (high Electron Gain Enthalpy), held together by strong electrostatic forces.
2. Covalent Bond: Mutual sharing of electron pairs between non-metals to achieve stability.
3. Coordinate (Dative) Bond: A special covalent bond where the shared electron pair is contributed entirely by one atom (the donor, acting as a Lewis Base) to another (the acceptor, acting as a Lewis Acid). Example: Formation of Ammonium ion ($NH_4^+$) from $NH_3$ and $H^+$.

core_concepts.title: Lattice Enthalpy
core_concepts.description:
The energy required to completely separate one mole of a solid ionic compound into its constituent isolated gaseous ions. Higher lattice enthalpy implies higher stability and higher melting point. It depends on two factors:
1. Charge on ions: Lattice Energy $\propto (q_1 \times q_2)$. (Dominant factor).
2. Size of ions: Lattice Energy $\propto 1 / (r_1 + r_2)$. Smaller ions form stronger lattices.

core_concepts.title: VSEPR Theory (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion)
core_concepts.description:
The 3D shape of a molecule is determined by the repulsions between electron pairs in the valence shell of the central atom. 
Order of repulsion: Lone Pair-Lone Pair (LP-LP) > Lone Pair-Bond Pair (LP-BP) > Bond Pair-Bond Pair (BP-BP).
This unequal repulsion causes bond angles to shrink from their ideal geometry when lone pairs are present (e.g., Ideal Tetrahedral is $109.5^\circ$, but $NH_3$ (1 LP) is $107^\circ$, and $H_2O$ (2 LP) is $104.5^\circ$).

important_entities.name: Formal Charge
important_entities.significance: Formal charge helps in deciding the most stable Lewis structure among various resonance structures. The most stable structure is generally the one where formal charges are closest to zero, and any negative formal charge resides on the most electronegative atom.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A massive source of errors in exams. 'Geometry' (or Electron Domain Geometry) includes BOTH lone pairs and bond pairs. 'Shape' (or Molecular Geometry) describes the visible positions of ATOMS only, ignoring the lone pairs. For example, $NH_3$ has a Tetrahedral GEOMETRY (4 electron domains), but a Trigonal Pyramidal SHAPE (3 atoms, 1 lone pair).

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
To instantly find hybridization and geometry without drawing Lewis structures:
$V$ = Valence electrons of central atom.
$M$ = Number of Monovalent atoms attached (like H, F, Cl. Do NOT count Oxygen!).
$C$ = Cationic charge (subtract it).
$A$ = Anionic charge (add it).
Result: 2=sp (Linear), 3=sp2 (Trigonal Planar), 4=sp3 (Tetrahedral), 5=sp3d (TBP), 6=sp3d2 (Octahedral).

exam_strategy_tips: When using VSEPR for molecules with multiple bonds (like $SO_2$ or $CO_2$), treat double and triple bonds exactly as a SINGLE super electron domain when determining geometry. The extra pi-electrons do not change the base geometry, though they do exert slightly more repulsion than a single bond.
